target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school calculus students

outline.target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school calculus students

sections.title: The Perspective Shift: From Slope to Stretch
sections.content: Introduce the idea that while derivatives are often seen as the 'slope of a tangent line' on a graph, they can also be viewed as a 'local scaling factor' between two number lines. This section transitions the viewer from the static x-y coordinate plane to a dynamic mapping perspective.
sections.example: Imagine two parallel horizontal number lines: an Input Line (x) and an Output Line (y). Instead of a curve, we draw 'mapping arrows' connecting points on x to points on y.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Linear Mapping
sections.content: Before tackling curves, understand how a linear function transforms space. If f(x) = 2x, every interval on the input line is stretched by a factor of 2 on the output line. This 'stretching constant' is the simplest form of a derivative.
sections.example: A 'Rubber Band' is stretched between two pegs on the input line. When mapped to the output line via f(x)=2x, the band becomes exactly twice as long, regardless of where it starts.

sections.title: The Local Scaling Factor
sections.content: For non-linear functions, the stretching isn't uniform. Introduce the derivative f'(x) as the specific 'zoom factor' at a single point. If you nudge 'x' by a tiny amount (dx), the output 'y' moves by dy. The derivative is the ratio: how much the space is being locally expanded or compressed.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Magnifying Glass' moving along the input line. Inside the glass, the mapping looks linear. The 'Magnification Power' printed on the glass is the value of the derivative at that spot.

sections.title: Application: The Square-Bot’s Journey
sections.content: Apply the transformational view to f(x) = x². Show that as we move further from the origin, the mapping arrows spread out significantly, meaning the 'stretching factor' (the derivative) is increasing.
sections.example: A character named 'Square-Bot' walks from x=1 to x=3. At x=1, a tiny step results in a step of size 2 (f'(1)=2). At x=3, the same tiny step on the input line causes a massive leap of size 6 on the output line (f'(3)=6). The space is being 'stretched' more aggressively as Square-Bot moves right.

sections.title: The Chain Rule: Compounding Stretches
sections.content: Demonstrate why this view makes the Chain Rule intuitive. If one function stretches space by 2 and the next stretches it by 3, the total stretch is the product (2 * 3 = 6).
sections.example: Two machines in a factory: Machine A stretches a piece of dough by f'(x), and Machine B stretches it again by g'(f(x)). The total change in length is the product of the two scaling factors.

sections.title: Summary and Intuition
sections.content: Summarize that f'(x) > 1 means expansion, 0 < f'(x) < 1 means compression, and f'(x) < 0 means the space is being flipped (mirrored) and stretched.
sections.example: A summary graphic showing a 'Density Map': where the derivative is high, input points are 'scattered' wide; where the derivative is low, input points are 'crushed' together.

storyboard.title: The Perspective Shift: From Slope to Stretch
lecture_lines: Derivatives are usually seen as slopes on a graph.
But we can view them as a local stretch.
Let's map input lines to output lines with arrows.
animations: Display a standard x-y coordinate plane with a curve and a tangent line at a point. Tangent line is #FFD700.
The x-y plane fades out. Two horizontal number lines appear: Input Line (x) top (#00BFFF), Output Line (y) bottom (#FF4500).
Draw mapping arrows (#FFFFFF) connecting several points on the Input Line to corresponding points on the Output Line.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Linear Mapping
lecture_lines: Consider the linear function f(x) equals two x.
Every interval on the input is doubled on output.
This constant stretch factor is the derivative's value.
animations: Focus on the two number lines. Show f(x)=2x at the top. A blue interval (rubber band) appears on the Input Line from x=1 to x=2.
Arrows map the start and end of the blue interval to y=2 and y=4 on the Output Line. A red interval appears on the Output Line, twice the length of the blue one.
Label the red interval 'Length = 2x Input' in #FFFF00. The number '2' flashes to emphasize the scaling factor.

storyboard.title: The Local Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: For curves, the stretching factor changes at every point.
Zoom into a tiny nudge, d x, on input.
The resulting nudge, d y, shows the local scaling.
The derivative is this specific local magnification power.
It tells us how much space expands or contracts.
animations: Two number lines. A non-linear mapping (arrows are not parallel). A small interval dx (#00FF00) appears on the Input Line.
A magnifying glass (#FFFFFF) appears over the dx interval. Inside the glass, the mapping arrows look parallel.
Show the corresponding dy interval on the Output Line. Label it 'dy' (#FF00FF).
The magnifying glass displays a number 'f\u0027(x) = 3' in #FFFF00. The dy interval is visibly 3 times larger than dx.
The formula dy = f\u0027(x) * dx appears, with f\u0027(x) highlighted in #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: Application: The Square-Bot’s Journey
lecture_lines: Let's apply this to f(x) equals x squared.
At x equals one, a small step doubles in size.
As Square-Bot moves right, the output steps grow larger.
At x equals three, the stretch factor becomes six.
The derivative tracks this increasing density of mapping arrows.
animations: A small character 'Square-Bot' (#00FF00) stands at x=1 on the Input Line.
Square-Bot takes a small step dx. The mapping arrow shows a step of 2*dx on the Output Line. A label 'f\u0027(1)=2' appears.
Square-Bot walks to x=3. The mapping arrows become steeper and more spread out.
Square-Bot takes the same tiny step dx. The mapping arrow shows a much larger step of 6*dx on the Output Line. Label 'f\u0027(3)=6' appears.
Highlight the Output Line from y=1 to y=9. Show how the density of points decreases as x increases.

storyboard.title: The Chain Rule: Compounding Stretches
lecture_lines: The chain rule is just compounding these local stretches.
Machine A stretches the input by a factor of two.
Machine B stretches that result by a factor of three.
The total stretch is the product: two times three.
We multiply the local scaling factors to find total change.
animations: Three parallel number lines: x (#00BFFF), u (#00FF00), and y (#FF4500).
A segment on x is mapped to a segment on u that is 2x larger. Label 'du/dx = 2' (#FFFF00).
The segment on u is mapped to a segment on y that is 3x larger than the u segment. Label 'dy/du = 3' (#FFFF00).
An arrow bypasses the middle line, mapping x directly to y. The segment on y is 6x larger than the x segment.
Display the formula (dy/du) * (du/dx) = dy/dx. The numbers 3 * 2 = 6 appear below.

storyboard.title: Summary and Intuition
lecture_lines: Values above one expand space; below one they compress.
Negative derivatives flip the orientation of the number line.
This transformational view makes calculus feel dynamic and intuitive.
animations: Show a segment on the input line being mapped to a larger segment (f\u0027>1) and then a smaller segment (0<f\u0027<1) on the output line.
Show arrows crossing each other as they map from the input to the output line, indicating a reflection (f\u0027<0).
A 'Density Map' appears on the Output Line: areas where arrows cluster (compression) and areas where they spread (expansion).
